items.stem: What is meant by the rate of a reaction?
options: the time taken for the reaction to finish
the total amount of product formed
the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time
items.answer: the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time
items.markingKey: Rate = Δ[conc]/Δt, e.g. mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.

items.stem: Explain why the gradient of a volume-of-gas against time graph decreases with time.
items.answer: As reactants are used up their concentration falls, so collisions are less frequent and the rate (gradient) decreases until it reaches zero.
items.markingKey: reactant concentration falls [1]; fewer collisions per second [1]

items.stem: Explain why 1/time can be used as a measure of rate in a "disappearing cross" experiment.
items.answer: The same amount of precipitate (sulfur) must form to obscure the cross each time, so rate ∝ amount/time ∝ 1/time.
items.markingKey: fixed amount of product [1]; rate ∝ 1/t [1]

items.stem: Lucas, a student in Nairobi, reacts hydrogen peroxide solution with manganese(IV) oxide catalyst and collects the oxygen in a gas syringe. Volume readings: 0 s: 0 cm³, 30 s: 26 cm³, 60 s: 45 cm³, 90 s: 59 cm³, 120 s: 70 cm³, 180 s: 83 cm³, 240 s: 91 cm³. Calculate the average rate of reaction between 60 s and 90 s.
items.answer: 0.467 cm³ s⁻¹
items.markingKey: volume change = 59 − 45 = 14 cm³ [1]; rate = 14/30 = 0.467 cm³ s⁻¹ [1]

items.stem: Mateo, a student in Muscat, reacts marble chips (calcium carbonate) with dilute hydrochloric acid and collects the carbon dioxide in a gas syringe. Volume readings: 0 s: 0 cm³, 30 s: 22 cm³, 60 s: 36 cm³, 90 s: 44 cm³, 120 s: 50 cm³, 180 s: 56 cm³, 240 s: 58 cm³. Calculate the average rate of reaction between 0 s and 30 s. Convert this rate into mol of gas per second (molar volume 24 000 cm³ at r.t.p.).

A class in Lagos follows the reaction of marble chips (calcium carbonate) with dilute hydrochloric acid using a gas syringe. (a) State two variables that must be controlled. (b) Suggest one source of error and an improvement.
items.answer: (a) Temperature; concentration/volume of acid; mass and particle size of solid. (b) Gas escapes before the bung is inserted (or the timer starts late): use a divided flask or tip the solid in after sealing; take readings at fixed time intervals.
items.markingKey: (a) Temperature; concentration/volume of acid; mass and particle size of solid. [2] (b) Gas escapes before the bung is inserted (or the timer starts late): use a divided flask or tip the solid in after sealing; take readings at fixed time intervals. [2]

items.stem: What are the units of rate when concentration is in mol dm⁻³ and time in seconds?
items.answer: mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
items.markingKey: Rate = Δc/Δt.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which measurement could follow the rate of CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂? (b) Why does the rate of reaction decrease as a reaction proceeds?
items.answer: (a) loss of mass of the flask over time (b) the concentration of reactants decreases
items.markingKey: (a) CO₂ escapes, so mass falls; or collect gas in a syringe. (b) Fewer reactant particles per unit volume, so fewer collisions per second.

items.stem: Explain why the final volume of gas is the same when the same mass of marble chips and powder react with excess acid.
items.answer: The same amount of CaCO₃ reacts, so the same amount of CO₂ forms; the powder only increases the rate.
items.markingKey: same amount of limiting reagent [1]; surface area affects rate only [1]

items.stem: A student in Mumbai claims that the rate of reaction is the total volume of gas produced divided by the time when the reaction stops. Is the student correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. That gives an average rate over the whole reaction; the rate at any instant is the gradient of the tangent.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: Nadia, a student in Singapore, reacts hydrogen peroxide solution with manganese(IV) oxide catalyst and collects the oxygen in a gas syringe. items.answer: 1.13 cm³ s⁻¹; 0.0000472 mol s⁻¹; reactant concentration is greater at the start, so more frequent collisions

items.stem: A class in Dhaka follows the reaction of hydrogen peroxide solution with manganese(IV) oxide catalyst using a gas syringe. (a) State two variables that must be controlled. (b) Sketch on the same axes the curve for the same mass of solid in smaller pieces, and explain.

items.stem: A class in Lisbon follows the reaction of calcium carbonate powder with dilute nitric acid using a balance (mass loss). (a) Describe how to find the initial rate from the graph. (b) Suggest one source of error and an improvement.
items.answer: (a) Draw a tangent at t = 0; gradient = Δy/Δx. (b) Gas escapes before the bung is inserted (or the timer starts late): use a divided flask or tip the solid in after sealing; take readings at fixed time intervals.

items.stem: Sipho investigates the rate of reaction between calcium carbonate powder and dilute nitric acid in a school laboratory, measuring the carbon dioxide produced. (a) Sketch the expected graph and explain its shape. (b) Describe how to find the initial rate from the graph.
items.answer: (a) Steep at first, gradient decreases, levels off when limiting reactant used up; concentration falls so fewer collisions. (b) Draw a tangent at t = 0; gradient = Δy/Δx.

items.stem: What is the activation energy of a reaction?
options: the average energy of the particles
the minimum energy that colliding particles need in order to react
the energy released by the reaction
the energy needed to melt the reactants
items.answer: the minimum energy that colliding particles need in order to react
items.markingKey: Ea: minimum energy for a successful collision.

items.stem: Use the Boltzmann distribution to explain why increasing the temperature increases the rate of reaction.
items.answer: At higher temperature the curve shifts to higher energy, so a much larger proportion (area) of molecules have E ≥ Ea; more successful collisions per second.
items.markingKey: curve shift/more molecules above Ea [1]; more successful collisions per unit time [1]

items.stem: Explain why the Boltzmann distribution curve never meets the energy axis at high energies.
items.answer: There is always a very small number of molecules with very high energy; there is no maximum energy.
items.markingKey: some molecules with very high energy [1]; no upper limit [1]

items.stem: For a reaction, 2.0% of molecules have energy ≥ Ea at 310 K and 4.0% at 330 K. Calculate the factor by which the number of molecules able to react increases, and use the Boltzmann distribution to explain why a 20 K rise has such a large effect.
items.answer: factor 2.0; the curve shifts to higher energies so the area beyond Ea increases greatly
items.markingKey: factor = 4.0/2.0 = 2.0 [1]; curve flatter and shifted right [1]; much greater area beyond Ea [1]

items.stem: For a reaction, 1.0% of molecules have energy ≥ Ea at 350 K and 2.5% at 370 K. Calculate the factor by which the number of molecules able to react increases, and use the Boltzmann distribution to explain why a 20 K rise has such a large effect.
items.answer: factor 2.5; the curve shifts to higher energies so the area beyond Ea increases greatly
items.markingKey: factor = 2.5/1.0 = 2.5 [1]; curve flatter and shifted right [1]; much greater area beyond Ea [1]

items.stem: For a reaction, 2.5% of molecules have energy ≥ Ea at 300 K and 7.5% at 310 K. Calculate the factor by which the number of molecules able to react increases, and use the Boltzmann distribution to explain why a 10 K rise has such a large effect.
items.answer: factor 3.0; the curve shifts to higher energies so the area beyond Ea increases greatly
items.markingKey: factor = 7.5/2.5 = 3.0 [1]; curve flatter and shifted right [1]; much greater area beyond Ea [1]

items.stem: A research group in Lisbon studies how temperature affects a reaction between gases, at 300 K and 320 K. (a) Sketch the Boltzmann distribution for the gas at both temperatures, labelling the axes. (b) Mark the activation energy and shade the region showing molecules that can react at the higher temperature.
items.answer: (a) y: number of molecules with energy E; x: energy. 320 K curve lower peak, shifted right; same area; both start at origin. (b) Ea on x-axis to the right of the peak; area under the curve to the right of Ea shaded.
items.markingKey: (a) y: number of molecules with energy E; x: energy. 320 K curve lower peak, shifted right; same area; both start at origin. [3] (b) Ea on x-axis to the right of the peak; area under the curve to the right of Ea shaded. [1]

items.answer: (a) Ea on x-axis to the right of the peak; area under the curve to the right of Ea shaded. (b) Greater proportion of molecules with E ≥ Ea; more frequent successful collisions. (c) More molecules per unit volume → more frequent collisions; energy distribution unchanged.

items.stem: In the Boltzmann distribution, what does the area under the curve represent?
items.answer: the total number of molecules
items.markingKey: Area is constant at different temperatures for the same sample.

items.stem: How does the Boltzmann distribution change when temperature increases?
options: the peak moves to the left and is higher
the area under the curve increases
the peak moves to the right and is lower; more molecules have E ≥ Ea
items.answer: the peak moves to the right and is lower; more molecules have E ≥ Ea
items.markingKey: Same area; broader curve shifted to higher energy.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In the Boltzmann distribution, what does the area under the curve represent? (b) How does the Boltzmann distribution change when temperature increases?
items.answer: (a) the total number of molecules (b) the peak moves to the right and is lower; more molecules have E ≥ Ea
items.markingKey: (a) Area is constant at different temperatures for the same sample. (b) Same area; broader curve shifted to higher energy.

items.stem: Explain why increasing concentration increases rate but does not change the proportion of successful collisions.
items.answer: More particles per unit volume give more frequent collisions, but the energy distribution (temperature) is unchanged so the fraction with E ≥ Ea is the same.
items.markingKey: more frequent collisions [1]; same fraction above Ea [1]

items.stem: In a test answer, Kenji states: "At a higher temperature the area under the Boltzmann curve increases." Explain why this statement is incorrect.

items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?
options: it makes the reaction more exothermic
it increases the energy of the molecules
it provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy
items.answer: it provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy
items.markingKey: More molecules have E ≥ the lower Ea.

items.stem: Use the Boltzmann distribution to explain how a catalyst increases the rate of reaction.
items.answer: The catalyst lowers Ea; the curve is unchanged, but a greater proportion of molecules now has energy ≥ Ea, so more successful collisions per second.
items.markingKey: Ea lowered, curve same [1]; more molecules above Ea [1]

items.stem: Explain why catalysts are important in industry.
items.answer: They allow reactions at lower temperatures, saving energy and cost, and can increase selectivity; they are not used up so small amounts work for a long time.
items.markingKey: lower temperature/energy saving [1]; reused/not used up [1]

items.stem: A reaction has ΔH = +90 kJ mol⁻¹. Its activation energy is 210 kJ mol⁻¹ uncatalysed and 165 kJ mol⁻¹ with a catalyst. Sketch a reaction pathway diagram showing both routes and calculate the activation energy of the catalysed reverse reaction.
items.answer: Ea(reverse, catalysed) = 75 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: products above reactants, ΔH labelled [1]; two humps, catalysed lower [1]; Ea(rev) = 165 − (+90) = 75 kJ mol⁻¹ [1]

items.stem: What is a homogeneous catalyst?

a catalyst that is used up

items.stem: Explain why a heterogeneous catalyst is often used as a fine powder or a mesh.

items.stem: Yusuf investigates the rate of reaction between hydrogen peroxide solution and manganese(IV) oxide catalyst in a school laboratory, measuring the oxygen produced. (a) Draw a labelled diagram of suitable apparatus. (b) Sketch on the same axes the curve for the same mass of solid in smaller pieces, and explain.
items.answer: (a) Conical flask with bung and delivery tube to gas syringe; stopwatch. (b) Steeper initially, same final volume; greater surface area, more frequent collisions.
items.markingKey: (a) Conical flask with bung and delivery tube to gas syringe; stopwatch. [2] (b) Steeper initially, same final volume; greater surface area, more frequent collisions. [2]

items.stem: Why does a small rise in temperature cause a large increase in rate?
options: the proportion of molecules with energy greater than Ea increases greatly
collision frequency doubles for every 10 °C rise
items.answer: the proportion of molecules with energy greater than Ea increases greatly
items.markingKey: Main effect: many more successful collisions; frequency increases only slightly.

items.stem: A student in Karachi explains rates of reaction using collision theory. Use the Boltzmann distribution to explain why increasing the temperature increases the rate of reaction.
items.answer: At higher temperature the curve shifts to higher energy, so a much larger proportion (area) of molecules have E ≥ Ea; more successful collisions per second.
items.markingKey: curve shift/more molecules above Ea; more successful collisions per unit time [2]

items.stem: Explain, using collision theory, the effect on the rate of the reaction of hydrogen with iodine gas of adding a catalyst. Refer to the Boltzmann distribution where relevant.
items.answer: Rate increases: an alternative route with lower activation energy, so a greater proportion of collisions have E ≥ Ea. Boltzmann: the curve is unchanged but Ea moves to the left, so a larger area lies above Ea.
items.markingKey: effect on rate [1]; explanation in terms of collision frequency or energy ≥ Ea [1]; Boltzmann/proportion above Ea correctly referred to (or stated unchanged) [1]

items.stem: For a reaction, 1.5% of molecules have energy ≥ Ea at 350 K and 4.5% at 370 K. Calculate the factor by which the number of molecules able to react increases, and use the Boltzmann distribution to explain why a 20 K rise has such a large effect.
items.answer: factor 3.0; the curve shifts to higher energies so the area beyond Ea increases greatly
items.markingKey: factor = 4.5/1.5 = 3.0 [1]; curve flatter and shifted right [1]; much greater area beyond Ea [1]

items.stem: For a reaction, 1.0% of molecules have energy ≥ Ea at 298 K and 2.5% at 318 K. Calculate the factor by which the number of molecules able to react increases, and use the Boltzmann distribution to explain why a 20 K rise has such a large effect.
items.answer: factor 2.5; the curve shifts to higher energies so the area beyond Ea increases greatly
items.markingKey: factor = 2.5/1.0 = 2.5 [1]; curve flatter and shifted right [1]; much greater area beyond Ea [1]

items.stem: For a reaction, 1.5% of molecules have energy ≥ Ea at 300 K and 3.0% at 310 K. Calculate the factor by which the number of molecules able to react increases, and use the Boltzmann distribution to explain why a 10 K rise has such a large effect.
items.answer: factor 2.0; the curve shifts to higher energies so the area beyond Ea increases greatly
items.markingKey: factor = 3.0/1.5 = 2.0 [1]; curve flatter and shifted right [1]; much greater area beyond Ea [1]

items.stem: A research group in Kathmandu studies how temperature affects a reaction between gases, at 350 K and 400 K. (a) Explain why the rate increases with temperature. (b) Explain why increasing the pressure also increases the rate, but by a different mechanism.
items.answer: (a) Greater proportion of molecules with E ≥ Ea; more frequent successful collisions. (b) More molecules per unit volume → more frequent collisions; energy distribution unchanged.
items.markingKey: (a) Greater proportion of molecules with E ≥ Ea; more frequent successful collisions. [2] (b) More molecules per unit volume → more frequent collisions; energy distribution unchanged. [2]

items.stem: Lina studies a gas-phase reaction at 400 K and 450 K. (a) Sketch the Boltzmann distribution for the gas at both temperatures, labelling the axes. (b) Explain why the rate increases with temperature.
items.answer: (a) y: number of molecules with energy E; x: energy. 450 K curve lower peak, shifted right; same area; both start at origin. (b) Greater proportion of molecules with E ≥ Ea; more frequent successful collisions.
items.markingKey: (a) y: number of molecules with energy E; x: energy. 450 K curve lower peak, shifted right; same area; both start at origin. [3] (b) Greater proportion of molecules with E ≥ Ea; more frequent successful collisions. [2]

items.stem: What type of catalysis is amylase (an enzyme) in the breakdown of starch in saliva?
items.answer: biological (enzyme)
items.markingKey: amylase (an enzyme): biological (enzyme).

items.stem: Yusuf compares catalysed and uncatalysed decomposition of hydrogen peroxide. Explain why a heterogeneous catalyst is often used as a fine powder or a mesh.
items.answer: Reaction occurs on the surface; a large surface area gives more active sites.
items.markingKey: surface reaction; larger surface area [2]

items.stem: Ravi compares catalysed and uncatalysed decomposition of hydrogen peroxide. (a) Explain why catalysts are important in industry. (b) Explain why a heterogeneous catalyst is often used as a fine powder or a mesh.
items.answer: (a) They allow reactions at lower temperatures, saving energy and cost, and can increase selectivity; they are not used up so small amounts work for a long time. (b) Reaction occurs on the surface; a large surface area gives more active sites.
items.markingKey: (a) lower temperature/energy saving; reused/not used up [2] (b) surface reaction; larger surface area [2]

items.stem: A reaction has ΔH = +52 kJ mol⁻¹. Its activation energy is 127 kJ mol⁻¹ uncatalysed and 97 kJ mol⁻¹ with a catalyst. Sketch a reaction pathway diagram showing both routes and calculate the activation energy of the catalysed reverse reaction.
items.answer: Ea(reverse, catalysed) = 45 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: products above reactants, ΔH labelled [1]; two humps, catalysed lower [1]; Ea(rev) = 97 − (+52) = 45 kJ mol⁻¹ [1]

items.stem: A reaction has ΔH = +52 kJ mol⁻¹. Its activation energy is 172 kJ mol⁻¹ uncatalysed and 82 kJ mol⁻¹ with a catalyst. Sketch a reaction pathway diagram showing both routes and calculate the activation energy of the catalysed reverse reaction.
items.answer: Ea(reverse, catalysed) = 30 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: products above reactants, ΔH labelled [1]; two humps, catalysed lower [1]; Ea(rev) = 82 − (+52) = 30 kJ mol⁻¹ [1]

items.stem: Nadia is writing a report on the use of vanadium(V) oxide as a catalyst in the Contact process. (a) Explain what is meant by a catalyst. (b) Sketch a reaction pathway diagram for catalysed and uncatalysed routes. (c) Give two economic or environmental benefits of using the catalyst.
items.answer: (a) A substance that increases the rate of reaction without being used up, by providing an alternative route with lower Ea. (b) Two humps; lower for catalysed; same ΔH. (c) Lower temperature/energy use; less fuel burned so less CO₂; faster production; catalyst reused.
items.markingKey: (a) A substance that increases the rate of reaction without being used up, by providing an alternative route with lower Ea. [2] (b) Two humps; lower for catalysed; same ΔH. [2] (c) Lower temperature/energy use; less fuel burned so less CO₂; faster production; catalyst reused. [2]

items.stem: Why does the rate of reaction decrease as a reaction proceeds?
items.answer: the concentration of reactants decreases
items.markingKey: Fewer reactant particles per unit volume, so fewer collisions per second.

items.stem: Diego measures the volume of gas produced every 30 s during a reaction in a quality-control laboratory. Explain why the final volume of gas is the same when the same mass of marble chips and powder react with excess acid.
items.answer: The same amount of CaCO₃ reacts, so the same amount of CO₂ forms; the powder only increases the rate.
items.markingKey: same amount of limiting reagent; surface area affects rate only [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why 1/time can be used as a measure of rate in a "disappearing cross" experiment. (b) Explain why the final volume of gas is the same when the same mass of marble chips and powder react with excess acid.
items.answer: (a) The same amount of precipitate (sulfur) must form to obscure the cross each time, so rate ∝ amount/time ∝ 1/time. (b) The same amount of CaCO₃ reacts, so the same amount of CO₂ forms; the powder only increases the rate.
items.markingKey: (a) fixed amount of product [1]; rate ∝ 1/t [1] (b) same amount of limiting reagent [1]; surface area affects rate only [1]

items.stem: The concentration of the ester (followed by titration) falls from 0.200 mol dm⁻³ to 0.150 mol dm⁻³ in 50 s. Calculate the average rate of reaction, giving units.
items.answer: 0.00100 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

items.stem: A class in Dhaka follows the reaction of calcium carbonate powder with dilute nitric acid using a balance (mass loss). (a) Draw a labelled diagram of suitable apparatus. (b) Suggest one source of error and an improvement.
items.answer: (a) Flask with cotton-wool plug on a top-pan balance; stopwatch. (b) Gas escapes before the bung is inserted (or the timer starts late): use a divided flask or tip the solid in after sealing; take readings at fixed time intervals.

items.answer: at the origin
items.markingKey: No molecules have zero energy; the curve never meets the energy axis at high energy.

items.stem: Kwame studies a gas-phase reaction at 300 K and 320 K. (a) Mark the activation energy and shade the region showing molecules that can react at the higher temperature. (b) Explain why increasing the pressure also increases the rate, but by a different mechanism. (c) State why not all collisions with sufficient energy result in reaction.
items.answer: (a) Ea on x-axis to the right of the peak; area under the curve to the right of Ea shaded. (b) More molecules per unit volume → more frequent collisions; energy distribution unchanged. (c) Particles must also collide with the correct orientation.
